eras.label: Age of Exploration (c. 1500–1613)
eras.summary: European sailors charted the Maine coast in the early 1500s: Giovanni da Verrazzano sailed it in 1524 and Estêvão Gomes mapped it in 1525. Samuel de Champlain's surveys of 1604–05 named landmarks including Mount Desert Island. The era closes with the first permanent French and English settlement attempts at Saint Croix Island (1604) and Popham (1607).

eras.label: Early Settlement (1614–1675)
eras.summary: English fishing stations, fur-trading posts, and small coastal towns — York, Casco (Falmouth Neck), Pemaquid — grew along the Maine coast, while the French held the fortified trading post of Pentagoet at Castine. Settlements were small, scattered, and depended on trade with the Wabanaki. Growth halted in 1675 with the outbreak of King Philip's War.

eras.label: King Philip's War (1675–1678)
eras.summary: The war spread into Maine in 1676 with Wabanaki raids on English settlements from York to Pemaquid, culminating in the Northeast Coast campaigns of 1676–77. Black Point (Scarborough) was attacked twice and Fort Pemaquid destroyed; the fighting ended with the Treaty of Casco in 1678.

eras.label: King William's War (1688–1697)
eras.summary: The first of the French and Indian Wars pitted English Massachusetts Bay against New France and its Wabanaki allies in Maine. French and Native forces destroyed Fort Loyal at Falmouth Neck (1690), raided York (1692), and captured Fort William Henry at Pemaquid (1696), nearly depopulating the English frontier.

eras.label: Queen Anne's War (1702–1713)
eras.summary: The North American theater of the War of the Spanish Succession, fought between Britain and France with Native allies. French and Wabanaki forces struck English settlements along the Maine coast, while British campaigns targeted Acadia. The 1713 Treaty of Utrecht ended the war and ceded peninsular Acadia to Britain.

eras.label: Dummer's War (1722–1725)
eras.summary: A conflict between New England and the Wabanaki Confederacy, sparked by English settlement expansion along the Kennebec River after Queen Anne's War. French Jesuit missionaries encouraged Abenaki resistance, and the English responded by building frontier forts and launching the 1724 raid that destroyed Norridgewock.

eras.label: King George's War (1744–1748)
eras.summary: The North American theater of the War of the Austrian Succession. After New England forces captured the French fortress of Louisbourg in 1745, the Wabanaki retaliated with raids on the Maine frontier. The war ended with the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, which returned Louisbourg to France.

eras.label: French and Indian War (1754–1763)
eras.summary: The North American theater of the Seven Years' War, pitting Britain against France and their respective Native allies. Massachusetts built a chain of forts up the Kennebec and along the coast to secure the Maine frontier. Britain's victory ended French rule in North America with the 1763 Treaty of Paris.

eras.label: Revolutionary War (1775–1783)
eras.summary: Maine was the northeastern frontier of the Revolution, then the District of Maine under Massachusetts. Coastal towns saw naval raids and British attacks, including the burning of Falmouth and the disastrous Penobscot Expedition. A fort on the Kennebec served as the launch point for Benedict Arnold's 1775 march to Quebec.

eras.label: War of 1812 (1812–1815)
eras.summary: During the War of 1812, Britain raided Maine's coast and briefly occupied eastern Maine as the colony of 'New Ireland.' The American frigate USS Adams was destroyed at Hampden, and the Enterprise captured HMS Boxer off Pemaquid Point. The defeat at Hampden and the occupation helped fuel the movement for Maine statehood.

eras.label: Early Statehood (1820–1860)
eras.summary: Maine became a state in 1820 under the Missouri Compromise. The new state built its capitol in Augusta and faced a bloodless border crisis with Britain in the Aroostook War, which the 1842 Webster–Ashburton Treaty settled by fixing Maine's northern border. Maine also passed the nation's first statewide prohibition law in 1851.

eras.label: Civil War (1861–1865)
eras.summary: Maine sent more soldiers per capita to the Union army than any other state. Its 20th Maine Volunteer Infantry became famous at Gettysburg under Brewer-born Joshua Chamberlain. Meanwhile, granite forts were built or completed to guard Maine's harbors, including Fort Gorges in Portland Harbor.

eras.label: Industrial Era (1860–1919)
eras.summary: Maine's timber, textile, and shipbuilding industries boomed after the Civil War, drawing French-Canadian mill workers to Lewiston and other mill towns. The Great Fire of 1866 rebuilt Portland in brick and stone, while iron shipyards at Bath and Kittery laid the groundwork for a century of naval construction.

eras.label: World Wars (1914–1945)
eras.summary: Maine shipyards launched destroyers and submarines for both world wars, and the coast bristled with naval air stations and coastal defenses. The sinking of the submarine USS Squalus off the Isles of Shoals in 1939 — and the daring rescue of 33 survivors — remains one of the Navy's most famous peacetime disasters.

eras.label: Cold War (1945–1991)
eras.summary: Strategic Air Command bombers stood nuclear alert at Loring AFB in Limestone, one of the closest U.S. bases to the Soviet Union, while Dow AFB in Bangor hosted interceptors and BOMARC missiles. Bath Iron Works built the Navy's guided-missile destroyers through the era's end.

eras.label: Modern Maine (1991–present)
eras.summary: After the Cold War bases closed, Maine reinvented itself around conservation, tourism, and civic firsts. Voters made Maine the first state to adopt ranked-choice voting in 2016, and the same year Katahdin Woods and Waters joined Acadia as a national monument.

sites.name: Casco Bay — first European sightings
sites.summary: European ships reached the Maine coast in the early 1500s: Giovanni da Verrazzano sailed along it in 1524, and Portuguese explorer Estêvão Gomes mapped the coast in 1525. The name 'Casco' reportedly derives either from the Abenaki 'Aucocisco' (place of herons / marshy place) or from Gomes's 'Bahía de Cascos' (Bay of Helmets).

sites.name: Saint Croix Island (1604)
sites.summary: In 1604 Pierre Dugua, Sieur de Mons, established a French winter settlement on this island in the Saint Croix River, with Samuel de Champlain among the expedition. The winter of 1604–05 was cruel: 35 of the 79 men died, and the survivors moved on by summer, though the attempt marked the beginning of the French presence in North America.

sites.name: Mount Desert Island
sites.summary: Samuel de Champlain sighted this island in 1604 and named it 'Isle des Monts Deserts' (Island of the Desert Mountains) for its bare, rounded summits. It is the largest island on the Maine coast and today lies partly within Acadia National Park.

sites.name: Popham Colony / Fort St. George (1607)
sites.summary: Founded in 1607 at the mouth of the Kennebec River by the Virginia Company of Plymouth, this was the second English colony in New England, contemporaneous with Jamestown. Its colonists built the Virginia of Sagadahoc, the first ocean-going ship constructed in English America, before abandoning the colony after one harsh winter in 1608.

sites.name: Pentagoet (Castine)
sites.summary: A fortified French fur-trading post at Castine, center of trade with the local Abenaki from 1635 to 1654 and the effective western border of Acadia. It later passed through English hands and became the base of the Baron de Saint-Castin before being destroyed by Dutch raiders in 1674. The site is now a National Historic Landmark District.

sites.name: York (Old York)
sites.summary: An early English settlement on the York River, founded in the 1630s and chartered in the 1640s, long known as 'Old York.' It became one of the most important towns of the Province of Maine and the site of repeated conflict during the colonial wars.

sites.name: Falmouth Neck (Portland)
sites.summary: The peninsula of present-day Portland was first colonized by the English in 1632 as a fishing and trading village called Casco. When Massachusetts Bay absorbed the Province of Maine in 1658, the town's name changed to Falmouth.

sites.name: Pemaquid (Bristol)
sites.summary: An early English settlement, fishing, and fur-trading station near Pemaquid Beach, Bristol, established around 1610. It became a major regional flashpoint in the late-17th-century conflicts between English and French settlers and between settlers and the Wabanaki; its village and fortifications are now an archaeological site.

sites.name: Attack on Black Point (1676)
sites.summary: On October 12, 1676, during the Northeast Coast campaign, Wabanaki forces led by Chief Mogg (Mogg Hegon) laid siege to the garrison at Black Point (present-day Scarborough), then the easternmost English settlement. The garrison was abandoned by the colonists the same day.

sites.name: Destruction of Fort Pemaquid (1676)
sites.summary: During the 1676 Northeast Coast campaign, Wabanaki forces destroyed Fort Pemaquid, the English fortification guarding the fishing and trading settlement. The campaign swept the Maine frontier from York eastward during King Philip's War.

sites.name: Fort William Henry (1692–1696)
sites.summary: Built by Massachusetts in 1692 at Pemaquid, it was in its time the largest English fort in New England. In 1696 it was captured and destroyed by French forces under Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville during the Siege of Pemaquid. A reconstruction was built in 1908 and is now part of Colonial Pemaquid State Historic Site.

sites.name: Candlemas Massacre, York (1692)
sites.summary: On January 24, 1692 — Candlemas Day — French-allied Wabanaki under Chief Madockawando raided York, killing dozens of settlers including Rev. Shubael Dummer, burning buildings, and carrying many captives to New France. The settlement was later rebuilt on higher ground at what is today York Village.

sites.name: Battle of Falmouth (1690)
sites.summary: From May 16–20, 1690, French and Wabanaki forces under Hertel de la Fresnière and the Baron de Saint-Castin besieged Fort Loyal on Falmouth Neck (present-day Portland). The fort surrendered and the settlement was burned; Portland's peninsula was largely deserted for more than ten years.

sites.name: Northeast Coast campaign (1703)
sites.summary: The first major campaign of Queen Anne's War in New England, running August 10 to October 6, 1703. French forces under Alexandre de Beaubassin and Wabanaki allies attacked English settlements along the Maine coast from Wells to Casco Bay, destroying and abandoning several settlements.

sites.name: Northeast Coast campaign (1712)
sites.summary: Wabanaki raiding on Maine and New Hampshire frontier towns, including Kittery, Wells, Berwick, and York, during the spring and summer of 1712. The campaign was reportedly retaliation for the British capture of Port Royal in Acadia.

sites.name: Battle of Norridgewock
sites.summary: On August 23, 1724, New England militiamen under Captains Moulton and Harmon attacked the Abenaki village of Norridgewock at Old Point, now part of Madison. The village was destroyed and the French Jesuit missionary Sébastien Rale was killed; survivors fled north to Quebec.

sites.name: Fort St. George
sites.summary: A British colonial fort at present-day Thomaston on the St. George River, built in 1719-1720. It was attacked during Dummer's War, besieged for 30 days in 1723, attacked again in the 1745 Northeast Coast campaign, and targeted in a failed 1758 French expedition.

sites.name: Fort Richmond
sites.summary: A Massachusetts colonial fort built around 1721 on the western bank of the Kennebec River at present-day Richmond. It survived a 1722 siege during Father Rale's War and served as the staging point for the 1724 raid on Norridgewock; it was rebuilt in 1740 and dismantled in 1755.

sites.name: Northeast Coast campaign (1745)
sites.summary: From July 19 to September 5, 1745, the Wabanaki Confederacy retaliated for the British capture of Louisbourg by raiding Maine settlements from Berwick to St. George (Thomaston). Within two months there were 11 raids, with every frontier town reportedly attacked.

sites.name: Fort Frederick (Pemaquid)
sites.summary: Rebuilt in 1729-1730 by Colonel David Dunbar at Pemaquid on the ruins of Fort William Henry. During King George's War it was attacked in the 1745 Northeast Coast campaign and withstood two more attacks in 1747; it was decommissioned in 1759 during the French and Indian War.

sites.name: Fort Halifax
sites.summary: Built in 1754-1755 at the confluence of the Sebasticook and Kennebec rivers at Winslow, guarding Wabanaki canoe routes toward the St. Lawrence and Penobscot valleys. Its surviving blockhouse is reportedly the oldest blockhouse in the United States.

sites.name: Fort Pownall
sites.summary: A British fortification built May-July 1759 at Fort Point in Stockton Springs, at the mouth of the Penobscot River, named for Governor Thomas Pownall. It never saw action during the war and was destroyed during the American Revolutionary War to keep it from British hands.

sites.name: Burning of Falmouth
sites.summary: On October 18, 1775, a Royal Navy squadron under Captain Henry Mowat bombarded and burned Falmouth (present-day Portland) in retaliation for Patriot resistance. Much of the town was destroyed. Outrage at the burning helped push the Second Continental Congress to create the Continental Navy.

sites.name: Battle of Machias (1775)
sites.summary: On June 11–12, 1775, armed townsmen of Machias pursued the British schooner HMS Margaretta down the bay aboard the sloop Unity. After the Margaretta's commander was mortally wounded, she surrendered. It is remembered as the first naval battle of the American Revolution.

sites.name: Penobscot Expedition (1779)
sites.summary: In July–August 1779, Massachusetts sent a fleet and militia to retake Castine, where the British were building Fort George. Hesitation among the American commanders and the arrival of a British relief squadron turned the operation into a rout, with the American ships burned or scuttled up the Penobscot. It was among the worst American naval defeats of the war.

sites.name: Battle of Machias (1777)
sites.summary: On August 13–14, 1777, a British force under Commodore Sir George Collier tried to seize Machias, then a base for American privateers. Local militia, aided by Penobscot, Passamaquoddy, and Maliseet allies, prevented a landing and drove the raiders off.

sites.name: Capture of HMS Boxer (1813)
sites.summary: On September 5, 1813, the USS Enterprise under Lt. William Burrows captured the Royal Navy gun-brig HMS Boxer off Pemaquid Point. Both commanding officers were killed in the roughly half-hour fight. The two captains were buried side by side in Portland's Eastern Cemetery.

sites.name: Battle of Hampden (1814)
sites.summary: On September 3, 1814, a British force under Sir John Sherbrooke attacked Hampden to capture the damaged frigate USS Adams. The frigate was scuttled and burned to prevent capture, and Bangor surrendered the same day. The defeat helped fuel Maine's post-war push for statehood.

sites.name: British Occupation of Castine (New Ireland)
sites.summary: From September 1814 to April 1815, Britain occupied Castine and governed eastern Maine as the colony of 'New Ireland,' rebuilding Fort George and adding new forts. The occupation ended with the Treaty of Ghent. Customs revenues collected there — the 'Castine Fund' — later helped found Dalhousie University in Halifax.

sites.name: Maine Statehood (1820)
sites.summary: Maine became the 23rd state on March 15, 1820, under the Missouri Compromise, separating from Massachusetts. Augusta was designated the capital in 1827, and the Bulfinch-designed State House was completed in 1832. The marker is placed at the State House in Augusta.

sites.name: Fort Kent Blockhouse (Aroostook War)
sites.summary: Built in 1839 by Maine militia during the bloodless Aroostook War border dispute with New Brunswick, Fort Kent is the only surviving American fortification from the crisis. The log blockhouse at the confluence of the Fish and Saint John rivers is now the Fort Kent State Historic Site.

sites.name: Webster–Ashburton Treaty (1842)
sites.summary: Signed August 9, 1842, in Washington, D.C., the treaty settled the Maine–New Brunswick border, ending the Aroostook dispute. It awarded about 7,015 square miles of the disputed territory to the United States and the remainder to Britain. The marker sits on the Saint John River near Madawaska, which the treaty made the border.

sites.name: Maine Law (1851)
sites.summary: Passed June 2, 1851, the Maine Liquor Law was the first statewide prohibition statute in the United States. It was drafted at the urging of Portland mayor Neal Dow, the 'Napoleon of Temperance.' Twelve states soon copied Maine's 'dry' laws; the law was repealed in 1856 but prohibition was later re-enacted in Maine.

sites.name: Joshua Chamberlain — Brewer
sites.summary: Born in Brewer in 1828, Joshua L. Chamberlain became colonel of the 20th Maine Volunteer Infantry in 1863. His regiment's stand on Little Round Top at Gettysburg earned him the Medal of Honor. After the war he served as governor of Maine and president of Bowdoin College.

sites.name: Fort Gorges
sites.summary: Built from 1858 to 1865 on Hog Island Ledge in Portland Harbor, this granite fort guarded the harbor entrance during the Civil War. Advances in artillery made it obsolete before it was ever garrisoned or fired a shot. It is now a park, reachable only by boat.

sites.name: Fort Knox (Maine)
sites.summary: Construction on this granite fort on the Penobscot River at Prospect began in 1844, after the Aroostook crisis, and continued through the Civil War until 1869. Built to protect Bangor's lumber port, it was never fully armed. It is Maine's largest historic fort and a National Historic Landmark.

sites.name: Great Fire of Portland (1866)
sites.summary: On July 4, 1866, a firecracker sparked a blaze that destroyed most of Portland's commercial district — 1,800 buildings across 10 streets. The city rebuilt in brick and stone, giving Portland its Victorian streetscape.

sites.name: Lewiston Mills and Water Power System
sites.summary: Canals harnessing the Androscoggin River's Great Falls powered one of New England's largest textile complexes, drawing tens of thousands of French-Canadian workers to Lewiston-Auburn. The historic district preserves the mills, canals, and worker housing.

sites.name: Acadia National Park (est. 1916)
sites.summary: Established in 1916 from private land donations, Acadia was the first national park east of the Mississippi. It preserves Mount Desert Island's coastline, Cadillac Mountain, and miles of carriage roads.

sites.name: Portsmouth Naval Shipyard
sites.summary: Founded in 1800 on Seavey's Island in Kittery (despite the New Hampshire name), the yard built the Navy's first submarine commissioned in 1900 and the USS Squalus. It remains an active submarine overhaul facility.

sites.name: Bath Iron Works
sites.summary: Founded in 1884, BIW on the Kennebec River became one of the Navy's premier warship builders, launching destroyers through both world wars and the Arleigh Burke–class guided-missile destroyers of the modern fleet.

sites.name: USS Squalus sinking (1939)
sites.summary: Built at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard in Kittery, the submarine USS Squalus sank during test dives off the Isles of Shoals on May 23, 1939, drowning 26 men. Divers using the new McCann Rescue Chamber saved all 33 survivors; the boat was salvaged and recommissioned as USS Sailfish. The actual wreck site lies just south of the state line, so the marker sits at the nearest Maine point.

sites.name: Naval Air Station Brunswick
sites.summary: Built in 1943, NAS Brunswick flew anti-submarine patrols over the North Atlantic in World War II and later based P-3 Orion squadrons through the Cold War. It closed in 2011 and is now Brunswick Landing, a civilian airport and business park.

sites.name: Portland Head Light (1791)
sites.summary: Completed in 1791 and commissioned by George Washington, Portland Head Light is Maine's oldest lighthouse. During World War II the surrounding Fort Williams bristled with coastal artillery and the light was dimmed for blackouts.

sites.name: Loring Air Force Base
sites.summary: Built 1947–1953 near Limestone, Loring was a Strategic Air Command heavy-bomber base — among the closest U.S. bases to the Soviet Union — with B-36 and B-52 wings on nuclear alert. It closed in 1994 and is now Loring Commerce Centre.

sites.name: Dow Field / Dow Air Force Base (Bangor)
sites.summary: Taken over by the Army just before World War II as Bangor Army Air Field, the base became Dow AFB in 1948, hosting Strategic Air Command bombers, air-defense interceptors, and BOMARC nuclear-tipped missiles. It closed in 1968; the Maine Air National Guard's 101st Air Refueling Wing still flies from the field.

sites.name: Ranked-choice voting adopted (2016)
sites.summary: Maine voters approved Question 5 in 2016 with 52%, making Maine the first state to adopt ranked-choice voting. First used in the 2018 primaries, Maine became the first state to use it in a presidential election in 2020.

sites.name: Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument (2016)
sites.summary: On August 24, 2016, President Obama designated 87,563 acres of forestland east of Baxter State Park a national monument, donated by Elliotsville Plantation. It protects the East Branch of the Penobscot River watershed, moose and lynx habitat, and Wabanaki cultural landscapes.

sites.name: Fort Western
sites.summary: A fortified trading post built in 1754 by the Kennebec Proprietors at the head of navigation on the Kennebec River, at modern Augusta; its main building is described as the oldest surviving wooden fort in America. In September 1775, Benedict Arnold's 1,100-man expedition stopped here to repair bateaux and gather supplies before the wilderness march toward Quebec.

settlement_shading.label: English settlements by ~1650 (approximate)
settlement_shading.note: Approximate. A narrow coastal strip from York to Pemaquid; the interior remained Wabanaki territory / uncontrolled by colonists.

settlement_shading.label: Settled coast and Kennebec corridor by ~1725 (approximate)
settlement_shading.note: Approximate. English settlement pushed up the Kennebec toward Norridgewock, but the frontier was violently contested during Dummer's War.

settlement_shading.label: River valleys contested by ~1760 (approximate)
settlement_shading.note: Approximate. British forts secured the Kennebec and Penobscot valleys, but much of the interior remained uncontrolled Wabanaki territory.

settlement_shading.label: Disputed / uncontrolled northern Maine by ~1840 (approximate)
settlement_shading.note: Approximate. Northern Maine was claimed by both the US and Britain (the Aroostook dispute); settled by lumbermen but not firmly controlled until the 1842 Webster–Ashburton Treaty.

settlement_shading.label: Near-full settlement by ~1860 (approximate)
settlement_shading.note: Approximate. After the 1842 border settlement, farming and lumber towns spread across most of the state; only the far north woods remained sparsely settled.
